subcategory: tender South African daisy grown as a warm-season bedding annual

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and set out transplants once soil has warmed; in zones 9-11 it behaves as a short-lived perennial and can be sown or divided in fall instead.

directions: This Karoo-region daisy produces crisp white ray florets surrounding a sharply contrasting steel-blue to blue-black central disc, a color pairing that gives it its common name and sets it apart from the orange and bronze tones typical of hybrid Arctotis bedding mixes. The silvery, felted foliage signals its drought tolerance, so plant it in lean, fast-draining soil and resist the urge to overwater or overfeed, which quickly produces lax, flopping growth with fewer blooms. Flowers close in late afternoon and on overcast days, reopening fully only in bright sun, so give it the sunniest spot available. It is excellent in gravel gardens, raised beds, and containers where its need for sharp drainage is easiest to satisfy.

subcategory: tender woody-based Chilean perennial grown as a cool-season bedding or container shrub

planting.note: Sow or root cuttings well ahead of the season since this shrubby species needs months of growth before it flowers; set out once frost danger has passed and bring container plants under cover if winter temperatures drop much below the mid-20s Fahrenheit.

directions: Unlike the familiar potted florist calceolaria hybrids, this Chilean species is a genuinely woody-based shrub that can reach several feet in a single mild-climate season, covering itself in dense clusters of small, bright golden-yellow pouch-shaped flowers from summer into fall. Its coarsely toothed, somewhat sticky leaves have a resinous scent when brushed. Give it cool nights, bright but not scorching sun, and soil that drains well but never dries out completely, since it resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. In marginal zones treat it as a container shrub that can be moved under cover for winter, or take cuttings in late summer as insurance against a hard freeze.

subcategory: cold-hardy Patagonian alpine rock garden perennial

planting.note: Plant divisions or young pot-grown plants in spring into gritty, humus-poor, sharply drained soil; this species tolerates severe winter cold far better than summer heat and humidity, and generally needs an alpine house or scree bed outside cool, maritime climates.

directions: Collected from windswept Tierra del Fuego scree slopes, this diminutive species forms a low mat of fleshy leaves topped by curious pouch-shaped flowers whose white, tooth-like marginal projections and dark red-brown blotching have earned it a reputation as one of the strangest flowers in cultivation. It demands the opposite of lush garden conditions: lean, mineral soil, constant air movement, and cool temperatures even in summer, which makes it a staple of alpine house and trough growers rather than a plant for an ordinary border. Keep roots cool and never let the crown sit in wet, stagnant soil over winter. Division of established clumps in spring is far more reliable than raising it from seed.

subcategory: tender Andean tuberous climbing vine related to Alstroemeria

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil and provide a trellis, fence, or shrub to twine through; mulch heavily over winter in zone 8-9 or grow in a large container that can be moved to shelter.

directions: This high-elevation Andean vine twines by its leaf stalks rather than true tendrils, climbing through shrubs or up a support to produce rounded, pendant clusters of tubular orange-to-yellow flowers freckled with maroon speckling, closely resembling a climbing version of its florist relative Alstroemeria. It prefers the same cool-summer, bright-but-not-scorching conditions as other high-Andes Bomarea species and performs best where nights stay relatively cool even in the growing season. Give it a consistently moist, humus-rich root zone during active growth, then allow a drier rest once top growth dies back in fall. In regions with real freezes, grow it as a container vine wintered somewhere frost-free, bringing it back out once the risk of hard frost has passed.

subcategory: tender Mexican gesneriad grown from scaly rhizomes

planting.note: Start dormant rhizomes shallowly in a loose, humus-rich mix in spring, keeping them warm and just barely moist until shoots appear, then increase water and humidity as growth develops.

directions: In contrast to the more commonly offered orange and red-flowered Smithiantha hybrids, this species carries nodding, pure white, narrowly tubular flowers held well above its soft, velvety, dark-veined leaves on upright spikes in late summer and fall. Like other gesneriads grown from scaly rhizomes, it needs a distinct dormancy: once flowering finishes and foliage yellows, withhold water and store the rhizomes cool and dry until repotting the following spring. High humidity and bright, indirect light bring out the best leaf texture and most reliable bloom, making it better suited to a terrarium, humid greenhouse bench, or enclosed windowsill case than an open, dry room. Handle the brittle rhizomes carefully when repotting, since broken pieces can simply be potted separately to increase stock.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; propagate by softwood cuttings in early summer, since branches that touch the ground also root readily on their own.

directions: This low, mounding sport of cutleaf stephanandra stays only knee-high while spreading several feet wide, its finely crimped, deeply cut leaves forming a dense, weed-smothering mat that is noticeably daintier in texture than the full-sized species. Small white flowers appear along the arching stems in late spring but are secondary to the plant's foliage effect and self-layering habit. Fall color runs through shades of orange and red-purple before leaf drop reveals an interesting tangle of fine, zigzagging twigs useful for winter interest. Its sprawling, rooting branches make it a reliable bank or slope stabilizer in the difficult zone between tree roots and open lawn where few other shrubs perform as well.
